title: Our Need for the Atonement
focus: Practice topic: teaching the Atonement in two minutes
intro: The Atonement of Jesus Christ is at the center of God’s plan. In this lesson learners see why every person needs it, what blessings it brings, and how to teach it simply: explain it, share a scripture or an experience, and testify.
preparation: Study Romans 3:23, 2 Nephi 9:6–10 and Alma 42:9–14. Then read about the blessings of the Atonement in Mosiah 3:19, Mosiah 4:3, Mosiah 24:12–15, Alma 5:12–13 and Alma 7:11–13. Read the Bible Dictionary entry on Atonement. Pray for each learner by name.

sections.title: Why we need the Atonement
paras: Begin by asking: How does a person come to feel that he or she needs the Savior? Then ask what we mean by the Fall of Adam.

Explain that Adam and Eve partook of the fruit and were cast out of God’s presence. That was spiritual death. They also became mortal and subject to physical death. As their children we inherit this condition: we are apart from God’s presence, we face physical death, and we are tested by hard things and by temptation (see Alma 42:5–9, 2 Nephi 2:11–14).

Let learners study Romans 3:23, 2 Nephi 9:6–10 and Alma 42:9–14. Ask how each of us is affected by the Fall. Write their answers on the board: we all sin, sin separates us from God, we will all die, and we must overcome the natural man (see Mosiah 3:19).

Then show the answer. Through the Atonement we escape death and hell (see 2 Nephi 9:10). Everyone will be resurrected, and everyone who repents can be made clean. Without the Savior we would be lost. Bear a short testimony of the wisdom and mercy of God’s plan.

sections.title: Why teaching the Atonement matters
paras: Read this from Elder Richard G. Scott, “He Lives! All Glory to His Name!”, general conference, April 2010: “The Atonement gives all the opportunity to overcome the consequences of mistakes made in life.” Ask: Why is it important to understand the Atonement deeply, and how can a future missionary make it part of who he or she is?

Many young people think the Atonement is only about forgiveness. Give learners time to search Mosiah 3:19, Mosiah 4:3, Mosiah 24:12–15, Alma 5:12–13 and Alma 7:11–13 for other blessings. Write what they find on the board.

Read together 1 Nephi 8:10–12, Enos 1:5–9, Mosiah 27:34–36 and Mosiah 28:1–4. Ask what pattern they see. Each of these men tasted the Atonement and then wanted others to taste it too. Ask: How do your own experiences with the Atonement move you to share the gospel?

sections.title: Helping others receive its blessings
paras: Read 2 Nephi 2:6–8. Ask what Lehi taught we should do with our knowledge of the Savior’s sacrifice.

Elder Jeffrey R. Holland taught that missionaries often say they want people to be baptized, but forget what must come first: faith in the Lord Jesus Christ and repentance (“Missionary Work and the Atonement,” Ensign, March 2001). Read Doctrine and Covenants 20:37 and ask what a person should show before baptism.

Read Doctrine and Covenants 18:11–14. Ask: What is the most important thing a missionary can do to bring people to Christ? Why is repentance the only way to receive the full blessings of the Atonement (see Mosiah 16:13, Alma 11:37, Helaman 14:13)? Write this on the board: missionaries teach repentance so that people can receive the full blessings of the Atonement and begin a new life in Christ.

sections.title: Explain, share and testify
paras: Teach a simple pattern every missionary can use. First, explain a doctrine in your own words. Second, share a scripture or a personal experience that helps explain it. Third, bear testimony of how you feel about it and why it matters.

Then teach how to use scripture in three steps: introduce the passage, read it, and apply it. Show the steps yourself with Mosiah 3:16–19, so learners do not feel overwhelmed. Give a few minutes to prepare, then let learners teach each other.

steps.why: Teach the idea and why it matters for a missionary.

examples.title: Explain the Fall in plain words
examples.text: Write fall, spiritual death and physical death on the board. Ask learners to say what each means. Then give the simple answer: because of the Fall we are apart from God and we will die, and we need a Savior.

examples.title: Show what the Atonement gives
examples.text: Draw two columns: what the Fall brought, and what the Atonement gives. Fill them from 2 Nephi 9:6–10 and Mosiah 3:19. Show that everyone is resurrected and everyone who repents can be clean.

examples.title: Teach the three-part pattern
examples.text: Write three words: explain, share, testify. Say what each one means and why a missionary needs all three.

steps.why: Show one example of what learners will do.

examples.title: Teach the Atonement in two minutes
examples.text: Teach one learner about the Atonement. Explain in your own words, share Alma 7:11–13, and testify. Let the class see each of the three parts.

examples.title: Use a scripture in three steps
examples.text: Teach Mosiah 3:16–19 by introducing it, reading it and applying it. Keep it short so learners see that they can do it too.

examples.title: Answer a plain question
examples.text: Answer aloud: Why do I need a Savior? Use the Fall, one scripture and a short testimony.

steps.why: Learners practise in pairs or small groups.

examples.title: Teach in pairs
examples.text: Learners read about the Atonement, then each prepares a two-minute lesson: explain, share, testify. They teach a partner and then switch.

examples.title: Choose a scripture
examples.text: Each learner picks a passage about the Atonement that they understand and can testify of. They teach it to a partner in three steps: introduce, read, apply.

examples.title: Find the pattern
examples.text: In pairs, learners read 1 Nephi 8:10–12 and Enos 1:5–9. They explain to each other what happened after these men felt the blessings of the Atonement.

steps.why: Name what went well and what can improve.

examples.title: Partner feedback
examples.text: The learner who was taught says what was clearest. The teacher writes one thing to keep and one to improve.

examples.title: Three questions
examples.text: Ask: What went well? What could you make simpler? What helped the listener most to understand why we need the Atonement? Begin with the good.

examples.title: Simple checklist
examples.text: Was the doctrine in plain words? Was a scripture or experience shared? Was there a testimony? Did the listener understand?

steps.why: Practise again with what was learned.

examples.title: Switch roles
examples.text: The learner who listened now teaches. Leave time for feedback both ways.

examples.title: Improve one thing
examples.text: Each learner teaches again and changes one thing: a simpler word, a better scripture or a stronger testimony.

examples.title: Teach a new partner
examples.text: Find a new partner and teach again in two minutes. Share one thing you learned.

testimony: Invite learners to say how they feel about the Savior and His Atonement. Share your own testimony that He lives and that His gift is for everyone.

tips.text: Create a warm atmosphere. Greet each learner and show that you value them.
Ask learners often to explain a doctrine in simple words.
Model a skill before asking learners to try it, and keep your example short.
Leave time at the end for learners to share feelings, not only facts.

quote.text: The Atonement gives all the opportunity to overcome the consequences of mistakes made in life.
quote.by: Elder Richard G. Scott, “He Lives! All Glory to His Name!”, general conference, April 2010

study: Read 2 Nephi 2:6–8 together and ask what we should do with what we know about the Atonement.
invitations: During your scripture study, mark the passages that help you understand Jesus Christ and His Atonement.
Share your testimony of the Atonement with someone at home, at church or online.
Take a few minutes each day to study the Atonement in the scriptures.

blocks.text: Keep the review short. Let two or three learners share, and thank each one.
Welcome the class warmly. Begin with a prayer and a short thought from scripture to invite the Holy Ghost.
What happened when you tried last lesson’s invitation? Who would like to share?
Listen for: real experiences, effort made, one thing learned.
Try saying: “Before we start, who would like to tell us what happened when they tried last week’s invitation?”
Read the introduction aloud slowly. Then ask one learner to say it again in their own words.

Try saying: “Today we will learn, practise and then teach what we learned. Every one of you will teach.”
Let learners say how a person comes to feel this need. Their own words teach each other.

Time each learner: ninety seconds, three steps.

Teach the pattern: Explain, Share, Testify. Try it on the Atonement: “It cleans me. I read Alma 7:11–13. I know the Savior loves me.”

assignments: Read 2 Nephi 2:6–8 again at home. Write one thing it teaches you and be ready to share it.
Practise this topic with someone at home before next class: teaching the Atonement in two minutes.
